lessons.title: Contract law fundamentals
lessons.body:
## What makes a contract
A contract is a legally enforceable promise (or set of promises) between parties. On the exam you need to know the elements that make a contract **valid**, the ways contracts are classified, and what happens when something goes wrong with capacity or consent.

### The essential elements
Most textbooks list five elements for a valid real estate contract:

| Element | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Competent parties** | Each party has legal [[capacity]]: of legal age and mentally competent. |
| **Offer and acceptance** | A definite [[offer]] and an unconditional [[acceptance]] of those exact terms — often called *mutual assent* or a *meeting of the minds*. |
| **[[Consideration]]** | Something of legal value given or promised by each side: money, a promise to pay, a promise to convey. |
| **Legal purpose** | The object of the contract must be lawful. A contract to do something illegal is void. |
| **Writing (for real estate)** | Under the [[Statute of Frauds]], contracts to buy or sell an interest in real property must be in writing and signed by the party to be charged to be enforceable. |

The Statute of Frauds doesn't make an oral real estate contract illegal — it makes it **unenforceable** in court. In many states, leases longer than one year also must be in writing.

> **Exam tip:** "Good and valuable consideration" is enough. Courts generally don't weigh whether the price was fair — a "love and affection" gift deed is fine, but a sales contract needs real consideration from both sides.

### Classifying contracts
**By how they were formed**
- [[Express contract]] — terms are stated in words, oral or written. A listing agreement and a purchase contract are express.
- [[Implied contract]] — created by the parties' conduct. In many states, a broker who acts like a buyer's agent without a written agreement can create an implied agency relationship. (Colorado is different: by statute a broker is presumed to be a transaction-broker unless single agency is established by written agreement.)

**By who is bound**
- [[Bilateral contract]] — a promise for a promise; both parties are obligated. A purchase contract is bilateral (buyer promises to buy, seller promises to sell).
- [[Unilateral contract]] — a promise in exchange for an act; only one party is bound. An option is unilateral: the seller must sell if the buyer exercises, but the buyer doesn't have to buy. An open listing is often described as unilateral.

**By stage of performance**
- [[Executory contract]] — something remains to be done. A signed purchase contract before closing is executory.
- [[Executed contract]] — all parties have fully performed. After closing, the purchase contract is executed.

Don't confuse *executed* (fully performed) with *execute* meaning "sign." On the exam, "an executed contract" usually means fully performed.

### Legal effect
| Status | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Valid** | Has all elements; enforceable by both sides. | Signed purchase contract between competent adults. |
| **[[Void contract]]** | No legal effect at all; never was a contract. | Contract for an illegal purpose; contract with someone already declared incompetent by a court. |
| **[[Voidable contract]]** | Valid on its face, but one party may choose to cancel (disaffirm). Binding until that party acts. | Contract signed by a minor; contract induced by fraud or duress. |
| **Unenforceable** | Seems valid but a court won't enforce it. | Oral real estate sales contract; a claim brought after the [[statute of limitations]] ran. |

> **Exam tip:** Voidable is the "choice" status — only the protected party (the minor, the defrauded buyer) gets the choice. The other party stays bound.

### Minors and incapacity
- A contract with a **minor** is generally **voidable by the minor**, not by the adult. The minor can disaffirm before reaching majority or within a reasonable time after.
- A contract signed by someone a **court has already declared incompetent** is generally **void**; that person's court-appointed guardian must act for them, usually with court approval.
- Someone who is intoxicated or mentally impaired at signing, but not adjudicated incompetent, may be able to void the contract if they couldn't understand what they were doing.
- An agent signing for a principal needs proper authority. To sign a deed or contract for someone else, use a [[power of attorney]], typically recorded if used to convey real property.

### Defects in consent
Even with capable parties, a contract is defective if consent wasn't freely and knowingly given.

- **[[Misrepresentation]]** — a false statement of material fact the other party relied on. Innocent or negligent misrepresentation can still allow the victim to rescind.
- **[[Fraud]]** — an intentional misstatement or concealment of a material fact, made to induce the other party to act, that the other party reasonably relied on and was harmed by. Makes the contract voidable by the victim and can support damages. Brokers can also lose their license for it.
- **[[Duress]]** — forcing agreement through threats or force.
- **[[Undue influence]]** — taking unfair advantage of a position of trust or dominance (for example, a caregiver pressuring an elderly owner) to get an agreement.
- **Mistake** — a **mutual mistake** about a material fact (both parties believed the property included the parcel across the road) can make a contract void or voidable. A **unilateral mistake** by one party usually doesn't, unless the other side knew of it and took advantage. A mistake about the law, or about value ("I thought it was worth more"), generally isn't a defense.

**Puffing** — vague opinions like "best view in town" — is not misrepresentation because a reasonable buyer doesn't rely on it as fact. Stating "the roof is two years old" when it's twenty is a misrepresentation.

### Brokers and contract drafting
Brokers fill in forms; they generally may not practice law by drafting original contract language or giving legal advice. Colorado requires brokers to use Commission-approved forms when an appropriate one exists — another lesson covers those forms. When a client asks "Is this legally binding?" or "What are my legal rights?", the right answer on the exam is usually to recommend an attorney.

### Quick review
- Five elements: competent parties, offer and acceptance, consideration, legal purpose, writing.
- Bilateral = promise for promise; unilateral = promise for act.
- Executory = not yet performed; executed = fully performed.
- Minor's contract = voidable by the minor. Adjudicated incompetent = void.
- Fraud, duress, undue influence, misrepresentation = voidable by the victim.

lessons.title: Offers, acceptance and contract tools
lessons.body:
## How a contract comes together
Most contract questions on the exam are really timing questions: *When did the contract form? Was the offer still open? Who's bound?* This lesson walks through the life of an offer and the tools that modify or transfer a contract.

### Offer
An [[offer]] is a proposal that shows willingness to be bound on definite terms. The person making it is the **offeror**; the person receiving it is the **offeree**. In a home sale, the buyer is usually the offeror.

An offer ends when:
- It is **accepted** (it becomes a contract).
- It is **rejected** by the offeree.
- The offeree makes a [[counteroffer]].
- The offeror **revokes** it before acceptance is communicated.
- It **expires** by its own deadline or after a reasonable time.
- Either party **dies or becomes incompetent** before acceptance.
- The property is destroyed or the deal becomes illegal before acceptance.

### Revocation
An offeror can withdraw an offer **any time before acceptance has been communicated**, even if the offer says "open until Friday." Saying "I'll keep it open" without consideration doesn't bind the offeror. The exception is an [[option]], where the offeree paid consideration to keep the offer open.

### Acceptance and delivery
[[Acceptance]] must be:
1. **Unconditional** and match the offer exactly (the "mirror image" rule).
2. **Communicated** to the offeror or the offeror's agent, in the manner the offer requires.

Until the signed acceptance is delivered back, there is no contract and the offeror can still revoke. Delivery to the offeror's broker is generally treated as delivery to the offeror.

### Counteroffers
Any change to the terms — price, closing date, even a small item like keeping the refrigerator — is a **counteroffer**. A counteroffer:
- **Rejects and kills the original offer.** The original offeror can't later "accept" it unless the other side renews it.
- Is a new offer, with roles reversed.

> **Exam tip:** A seller who replies "I accept, but closing must be June 15 instead of June 1" has *not* accepted. That is a counteroffer, and the buyer's original offer is dead.

### Multiple offers
A seller can receive several offers at once. Key points:
- The listing broker must present **all** written offers to the seller promptly (unless the seller has given written instructions otherwise, where state law allows) — including offers that arrive after another offer is accepted, as backups.
- The seller chooses: accept one, reject all, or counter one (or more — but countering several at once risks two acceptances, so it should be done carefully and with clear language).
- The broker doesn't decide which offer is "best"; the seller decides. The broker may explain terms.
- A broker shouldn't disclose the terms of one buyer's offer to another buyer without the seller's permission, and must be honest — never invent "other offers."

A **backup offer** is accepted subject to the first contract failing.

### Electronic signatures
The federal **[[E-SIGN Act]]** (2000) and the **[[UETA]]**, adopted by nearly every state, give electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper ones, as long as the parties have agreed to do business electronically. Some documents may still require wet signatures or notarization under local recording rules, but purchase contracts and listing agreements can be signed electronically.

### Options
An [[option]] gives the **optionee** (often a buyer or tenant) the right, but not the obligation, to buy property at a set price within a set time. The **optionor** (owner) is bound to sell if the option is exercised.
- Requires separate consideration (the option fee).
- It's a unilateral contract until exercised; when exercised it becomes a bilateral purchase contract.
- The optionee may usually assign the option unless the contract forbids it.
- The option fee may or may not be credited toward the price — the contract says.

### Right of first refusal
A [[right of first refusal]] gives someone (often a tenant) the right to **match** a third-party offer before the owner sells to that third party. Unlike an option, there's no set price and the owner can't be forced to sell — the right is triggered only if the owner decides to sell.

### Assignment vs. novation
| | [[Assignment]] | [[Novation]] |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | A party transfers its rights (and usually duties) to someone else. | A new contract replaces the old one, often substituting a new party. |
| Original party's liability | **Remains** secondarily liable if the assignee fails to perform. | **Released** — the new party takes over completely. |
| Consent | Most contracts are assignable unless they say otherwise or are personal. | Requires agreement of all parties. |

Contracts for **personal services** (like a listing agreement, which depends on the broker's skill) generally can't be assigned without consent.

### Contingencies
A [[contingency]] is a condition that must be met before a party is obligated to perform. Common ones: financing (loan approval), appraisal, inspection, sale of buyer's current home, and title review. Good contingencies are specific: who, what, and by what deadline. If a contingency fails, the protected party can usually terminate without being in default, typically by giving written notice by the deadline.

### Time is of the essence
A [[time is of the essence]] clause makes deadlines strict: missing one is a breach, not just a minor delay. Without it, courts may allow a "reasonable time." Colorado's Commission-approved contracts include a time-of-essence provision, so deadlines in Colorado deals matter.

### Changing a contract: addenda and amendments
- An [[addendum]] is extra material made part of the contract **at the time it's signed** (e.g., a lead-based paint disclosure, a short sale addendum).
- An [[amendment]] **changes** an existing contract **after** it's formed (e.g., extending the closing date). All parties must sign it.

### Quick review
- Counteroffer = rejection + new offer.
- Revocation is allowed until acceptance is communicated.
- Option = right without obligation, needs consideration. Right of first refusal = right to match.
- Assignment leaves the assignor liable; novation releases the original party.
- Addendum = part of the original; amendment = later change.

lessons.title: Breach, remedies, purchase agreements and leases
lessons.body:
## When a party doesn't perform
A [[breach of contract]] is a failure, without legal excuse, to perform any promise in the contract. The exam focuses on which remedies fit which situation.

### Remedies at a glance
| Remedy | What the non-breaching party gets | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **[[Specific performance]]** | A court order forcing the breaching party to do what they promised. | Buyer sues a seller who refuses to close. Land is considered unique, so money may not be enough. |
| **Compensatory damages** | Money to cover the actual loss caused by the breach. | Seller resells for $20,000 less after buyer backs out. |
| **[[Liquidated damages]]** | An amount the parties agreed to in advance as the full damages for breach. | Seller keeps earnest money when buyer defaults. |
| **[[Rescission]]** | The contract is canceled and parties are put back where they started (deposits returned). | Contract induced by fraud or mutual mistake. |
| **Acceptance of breach** | The non-breaching party simply lets it go. | Seller decides not to pursue a buyer who walked away. |

> **Exam tip:** Specific performance is mainly a **buyer's** remedy against a seller, because each parcel of land is unique. Courts rarely force a buyer to buy; a seller usually seeks damages.

### Earnest money as liquidated damages
[[Earnest money]] is the buyer's good-faith deposit. Many purchase contracts let the seller keep the earnest money as liquidated damages if the buyer defaults. If the contract makes liquidated damages the seller's *sole* remedy, the seller can't also sue for more. Some forms let the seller choose between keeping the earnest money and pursuing actual damages. Liquidated damages must be a reasonable estimate — a court may refuse to enforce a sum that looks like a penalty.

Earnest money isn't required for a contract to be valid; the buyer's promise to pay is consideration. Brokers holding earnest money must handle it under their state's trust-account rules and can't simply hand it to one side in a dispute.

### Statute of limitations
Every state sets a [[statute of limitations]]: a deadline for filing a lawsuit for breach. After it runs, the claim is unenforceable. The length varies by state and by claim type, so the exam usually tests the concept, not a number.

### Discharge: how contracts end
A contract is **discharged** (ended) by:
- **Full performance** — the normal ending; the contract becomes executed.
- **Substantial performance** — most terms met; the other party may still owe payment minus damages for minor shortfalls.
- **Mutual agreement / release** — both parties agree to cancel.
- **Novation** — a new contract replaces the old.
- **Impossibility** — performance can't legally be done (property destroyed, a party dies in a personal-service contract).
- **Operation of law** — bankruptcy, statute of limitations, alteration of the contract without consent.
- **Breach** — releases the non-breaching party and opens up remedies.

## Purchase agreements
The purchase contract (sales contract, contract to buy and sell) is the most important document in most transactions. It identifies the parties and property (legal description), price and terms, financing, earnest money, deadlines, contingencies, inclusions/exclusions, title and closing provisions, possession, and default remedies. Until closing, it gives the buyer [[equitable title]] — an interest in the property even though the seller still holds legal title.

## Leases
A lease is both a conveyance of possession and a contract. The owner is the **lessor (landlord)**; the tenant is the **lessee**. The tenant holds a [[leasehold estate]], a non-freehold interest.

### Leasehold estates
| Estate | Key feature | Notice to end |
|---|---|---|
| **[[Estate for years]]** | Definite start and end date (any length, even six months). | None — ends automatically. |
| **[[Periodic tenancy]]** | Automatically renews period to period (month-to-month). | Notice required; period set by state law. |
| **[[Tenancy at will]]** | No set term; lasts as long as both want. | Ends on notice or death of either party. |
| **[[Tenancy at sufferance]]** | Tenant stays after the lease ends without the landlord's consent. | Lowest estate; landlord can evict. |

A sale of the property doesn't end an estate for years — the buyer takes subject to existing leases.

### Lease types (by how rent works)
| Lease | How it works | Typical property |
|---|---|---|
| **[[Gross lease]]** | Tenant pays fixed rent; landlord pays taxes, insurance, maintenance. | Residential, small office |
| **[[Net lease]]** | Tenant pays rent plus some of the property expenses. | Commercial |
| **[[Triple net lease]]** | Tenant pays rent plus taxes, insurance, and maintenance. | Freestanding retail, single-tenant commercial |
| **[[Percentage lease]]** | Base rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales (often above a threshold). | Retail, shopping centers |
| **[[Ground lease]]** | Tenant leases only land, usually long-term, and builds on it. | Commercial development |
| **[[Graduated lease]]** | Rent increases in scheduled steps. | Startups, long office leases |
| **[[Index lease]]** | Rent adjusts with an index such as the Consumer Price Index. | Long-term leases |

A **variable lease** is a general term for leases whose rent can change (graduated and index leases are examples).

### Percentage lease example
A retail lease calls for $2,000 per month base rent plus 4% of annual gross sales over $300,000. The store does $450,000 in sales. Overage = $450,000 − $300,000 = $150,000; 4% × $150,000 = $6,000. Annual rent = ($2,000 × 12) + $6,000 = **$30,000**.

### Lease-purchase and lease option
- **[[Lease option]]** — a lease plus an option to buy. The tenant may buy but isn't required to.
- **Lease-purchase** — the tenant agrees to buy; part of the rent is often credited to the price. Both sides are obligated to complete the sale.

### Assignment vs. sublease
| | Assignment of lease | [[Sublease]] |
|---|---|---|
| What transfers | The tenant's entire remaining interest. | Part of the interest (part of the space or part of the time). |
| Who pays the landlord | Assignee pays the landlord directly. | Subtenant pays the original tenant, who pays the landlord. |
| Original tenant | Stays liable unless the landlord releases them (novation). | Stays primarily liable. |
| Subtenant/assignee relation to landlord | Assignee is in privity of estate with the landlord. | Subtenant has no direct relationship with the landlord. |

### Quick review
- Land is unique → buyer can seek specific performance.
- Earnest money is often liquidated damages.
- Estate for years has a fixed end and needs no notice.
- Triple net: tenant pays taxes, insurance and maintenance.
- Sublease: original tenant is the subtenant's landlord.

lessons.title: Property disclosures and environmental hazards
lessons.body:
## Why disclosure matters
Under old common law the rule was [[caveat emptor]] — "let the buyer beware." Modern law in most states moved away from that. Sellers must disclose known material defects, and brokers have their own duty to disclose material facts they know about, regardless of whom they represent. Failing to disclose can lead to rescission, damages, and license discipline.

### Material facts
A [[material fact]] is one that would affect a reasonable person's decision to buy or the price they'd pay. Examples: a leaking roof, foundation cracks, a pending special assessment, flooding history, a planned highway next door, title problems.

### Latent vs. patent defects
- A [[latent defect]] is hidden — not discoverable by ordinary inspection (a cracked slab under carpet, a buried oil tank). Sellers and brokers who know about latent defects must disclose them.
- A **patent defect** is visible on reasonable inspection (a broken window, a stained ceiling). Buyers are expected to notice obvious problems, but brokers still shouldn't misrepresent them.

Never conceal a defect — painting over water stains or rearranging furniture to hide cracks turns nondisclosure into fraud.

### Seller disclosure forms
Most states use a seller property disclosure statement listing the condition of systems, structure, and known problems. The seller fills it out based on actual knowledge; the broker shouldn't complete it for the seller. Colorado's Commission-approved contracts call for a Seller's Property Disclosure on a Commission form, and the seller has a continuing duty to disclose newly discovered adverse material facts before closing.

A disclosure form is **not a warranty** and **not a substitute for an inspection**.

### Stigmatized property
A [[stigmatized property]] is one that buyers may avoid for psychological reasons — a murder or suicide on the premises, a former occupant with HIV/AIDS, reputed hauntings. These aren't physical defects. Many states say these facts are not material and need not be disclosed. In Colorado, C.R.S. 38-35.5-101 provides that facts or suspicions that a property was the site of a homicide, other felony, or suicide, or that an occupant had HIV/AIDS or another disease very unlikely to spread through occupancy, are not material facts that must be disclosed. Separately, under federal fair housing law, volunteering or answering questions about an occupant's HIV/AIDS status or other disability can be treated as disability discrimination.

### Recommending inspections and surveys
Brokers aren't inspectors. When a broker sees a red flag, the safe course is to disclose what you observed and recommend that the buyer get an expert. Recommend:
- A **home inspection** on virtually every purchase.
- A **survey** when boundaries, encroachments, fences, or easements are questionable.
- **Specialized inspections** — structural engineer, sewer scope, radon, mold, well and septic — when facts point that way.

### Red flags
Things a broker should notice and point out: water stains, musty smells, fresh paint in one spot, cracks in foundation or walls, sloping floors, doors that stick, efflorescence on basement walls, nearby landfills or industrial sites, fill dirt, pipes coming out of the ground (possible underground tank), and unpermitted additions.

## Environmental hazards
### Lead-based paint
The federal [[lead-based paint disclosure]] rule (EPA/HUD) covers most housing built **before 1978**. Before the buyer or tenant is bound by a contract or lease, the seller or landlord must:
- Give the EPA pamphlet *Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home*.
- Disclose known lead-based paint and hazards and provide available records and reports.
- Include a Lead Warning Statement in an attachment to the sales contract (for a lease, in the lease or attached to it).
- Give **buyers** a **10-day** opportunity to conduct a lead inspection or risk assessment. The parties can agree in writing to a different period, and the buyer can waive it in writing. (Tenants don't get this 10-day right.)
- Keep signed disclosure records for **3 years** after the sale closes or the lease begins.

**Agents** must tell sellers and landlords about these obligations and share responsibility for compliance. Exemptions include housing built after 1977; zero-bedroom units (studios, efficiencies, dorms) and housing for the elderly or disabled, unless a child under six lives or is expected to live there; short leases of 100 days or less with no renewal or extension; leases of units a certified inspector has found free of lead-based paint; and foreclosure sales.

### Radon
[[Radon]] is a naturally occurring, odorless, colorless radioactive gas from the decay of uranium in soil and rock. The EPA calls it the second leading cause of lung cancer (the leading cause among nonsmokers). The EPA recommends fixing a home at or above **4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L)**. Testing is simple; mitigation often uses sub-slab depressurization (a vent pipe and fan). Colorado has many high-radon areas.

### Asbestos
[[Asbestos]] was used in insulation, flooring, siding, and pipe wrap. It's dangerous when **friable** — crumbling and releasing fibers. Often the safest approach is to leave intact material alone or **encapsulate** it; removal can release more fibers and should be done by licensed professionals.

### Mold
Mold grows wherever there's moisture. Fixing the water source is essential. Musty odors and stains are red flags; recommend an inspection.

### Underground storage tanks
[[Underground storage tanks]] (USTs) holding fuel oil, gasoline, or chemicals can leak and contaminate soil and groundwater. Clues: fill or vent pipes sticking out of the ground, old gas stations, and older homes once heated with oil.

### Urea-formaldehyde
[[Urea-formaldehyde foam insulation]] (UFFI) was installed in the 1970s and can release formaldehyde gas. Formaldehyde also appears in some pressed-wood products and can cause respiratory irritation.

### Wetlands
[[Wetlands]] are protected under the federal Clean Water Act. Filling or building in them typically requires a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Wetlands can make part of a parcel unbuildable — a material fact for land buyers.

### CERCLA (Superfund)
[[CERCLA]] — the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act — lets the EPA clean up contaminated sites and recover costs. Liability is:
- **Strict** — no fault required.
- **Joint and several** — any one responsible party can be made to pay the whole cleanup.
- **Retroactive** — applies to contamination before the law was passed.

Current owners can be liable even if a prior owner caused the contamination. Commercial buyers commonly order a **[[Phase I environmental site assessment]]** to support the innocent landowner (and similar) defenses.

## Flood zones
FEMA's flood maps identify [[special flood hazard areas]] — land with a 1% annual chance of flooding (the "100-year floodplain"), labeled Zones A and V. If a property in one of these areas is financed with a federally backed or federally regulated loan, **flood insurance is required**. Location in a flood zone is a material fact, and a "100-year flood" can happen in back-to-back years.

Other flood basics:
- Standard homeowners policies **don't cover flood damage**; coverage comes from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) or private flood insurers.
- NFIP policies generally have a **30-day waiting period** before coverage starts, except when the policy is bought in connection with making, increasing, extending or renewing a loan (plus a few narrow exceptions, such as a purchase within a year after a flood map revision).
- Owners outside a mapped high-risk zone can still buy flood insurance, and many flood claims come from outside those zones.

> **Exam tip:** When a question asks what a broker should do about a suspected hazard, the answer is almost always: disclose what you know and recommend an expert inspection — never assure the buyer it's fine, and never conduct the test yourself as an expert.

questions.stem: Which element is required for a real estate sales contract to be enforceable, but is NOT required for most other contracts?
choices: A writing signed by the party to be charged
questions.explanation: The Statute of Frauds requires contracts for the sale of real property to be in writing to be enforceable. Consideration, capacity and legal purpose are required for every valid contract.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old signs a contract to buy a condo. Which describes the contract?
choices: Valid and binding on both parties
questions.explanation: A contract with a minor is generally voidable at the minor's option. The adult seller stays bound unless the minor disaffirms.

questions.stem: A contract signed by a person who had previously been declared incompetent by a court is
choices: unenforceable only after the statute of limitations runs
questions.explanation: Once a court has adjudicated a person incompetent, that person's contracts are generally void; a court-appointed guardian must act for them.

questions.stem: A buyer and seller orally agree on the sale of a house, and the seller later refuses to sign anything. The oral agreement is
choices: void because it has an illegal purpose
questions.explanation: Under the Statute of Frauds, an oral contract for the sale of real estate generally can't be enforced in court. It isn't illegal, just unenforceable.

questions.stem: A signed purchase contract where the parties are waiting for the closing date is best described as
questions.explanation: An executory contract still has obligations left to perform. It becomes executed when closing is complete and everything has been performed.

questions.stem: Which contract is unilateral?
choices: An option to purchase before it is exercised
A purchase contract signed by buyer and seller
questions.explanation: An option binds only the optionor (the owner) to sell; the optionee may choose not to buy. The other choices exchange promises for promises, so they're bilateral.

questions.stem: A seller tells a buyer the basement has never flooded, knowing it floods every spring. The buyer relies on this and buys. The contract is
choices: unenforceable under the Statute of Frauds
voidable by the buyer because of fraud
questions.explanation: An intentional misstatement of a material fact that the buyer relied on is fraud, which makes the contract voidable at the victim's option and can support damages.

questions.stem: An elderly owner sells her home well below market to her live-in caregiver, who had pressured her for weeks and controlled her finances. The owner's heirs would most likely challenge the sale on grounds of
questions.explanation: Undue influence is unfair use of a position of trust or control to obtain consent. Duress involves threats or force.

questions.stem: A buyer offers $410,000. The seller signs and returns the offer but changes the closing date by one week. What is the legal status?
choices: The seller has rejected the offer and made a counteroffer
A binding contract exists at $410,000 with the new date
A binding contract exists with the original closing date
The buyer's offer remains open for the seller to accept later
questions.explanation: Any change to the terms is a counteroffer, which rejects the original offer. No contract exists unless the buyer accepts the counteroffer.

questions.stem: On Monday a buyer makes an offer that says it will stay open until Friday at 5 p.m. On Wednesday, before the seller has accepted, the buyer withdraws it. Which is correct?
choices: The buyer stays bound until Friday at 5 p.m. because the offer stated that deadline
The seller can still accept the offer at any time up until Friday at 5 p.m.
The withdrawal is effective because no acceptance had been communicated
The buyer forfeits the earnest money by withdrawing before the stated deadline
questions.explanation: An offeror can revoke any time before acceptance is communicated. A promise to keep an offer open isn't binding without consideration, as in an option.

questions.stem: A seller signs a buyer's offer exactly as written at 3 p.m. The buyer phones the listing broker at 3:30 p.m. to withdraw, before learning of the signature. The seller's broker emails the signed contract to the buyer's broker at 4 p.m. Which is most likely true?
choices: A contract formed at 3 p.m., when the seller signed the offer exactly as written
The offer was revoked because acceptance had not yet been communicated
A contract formed at 4 p.m., when the signed offer was emailed to the buyer's broker
The seller can now choose whether or not a binding contract exists
questions.explanation: Acceptance must be communicated to the offeror or the offeror's agent. Because the buyer revoked before the signed acceptance was delivered, no contract formed.

questions.stem: A listing broker receives three offers on the same afternoon. What should she do?
choices: Present the offers one at a time, waiting for a response to each
Tell each buyer what the other offers contain so they can improve them
Present all three offers to the seller promptly
questions.explanation: Brokers must present all offers promptly so the seller can decide. Sharing one buyer's terms with others requires the seller's permission.

questions.stem: Under the federal E-SIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, an electronically signed purchase contract is
choices: valid only after each party's electronic signature has been notarized by a notary
unenforceable under the Statute of Frauds because no paper copy was ever signed
valid only if both parties also sign a paper copy within ten days of acceptance
as valid as a paper contract if the parties agreed to deal electronically
questions.explanation: E-SIGN and UETA give electronic signatures and records the same effect as handwritten ones when the parties have agreed to conduct business electronically.

questions.stem: A tenant pays the owner $3,000 for the right to buy the property for $500,000 at any time in the next year. The tenant is the
questions.explanation: The optionee holds the right to buy and pays for it. The owner who grants the option is the optionor and is bound to sell if the option is exercised.

questions.stem: A commercial tenant's lease says that if the owner receives an acceptable offer from a third party, the tenant may buy on the same terms. This provision is a(n)
questions.explanation: A right of first refusal lets the holder match a third-party offer. An option sets a price and lets the holder buy whenever they choose within the term.

questions.stem: A buyer assigns his purchase contract to a friend, and the seller does not release him. If the friend fails to close, the original buyer is
choices: liable only if he received a fee for the assignment
entitled to the friend's earnest money
questions.explanation: In an assignment the assignor remains secondarily liable. Only a novation, which substitutes a new party with everyone's agreement, releases the original party.

questions.stem: A seller agrees to let a new buyer replace the original buyer in a contract and releases the original buyer from all obligations. This is
questions.explanation: Novation substitutes a new contract or party and releases the original one. An assignment leaves the assignor liable.

questions.stem: After a contract is signed, the buyer and seller agree to move the closing date back two weeks. The document they sign is a(n)
questions.explanation: An amendment changes an existing contract after it is formed. An addendum is material made part of the contract when it is first signed.

questions.stem: A purchase contract says "time is of the essence." The buyer delivers the loan approval two days after the contract deadline. Which is most likely true?
choices: The buyer has a reasonable time after the deadline to perform
The deadline is only a goal and has no legal effect
The buyer is in breach for missing the deadline
questions.explanation: A time-is-of-the-essence clause makes deadlines strict, so missing one is a breach. Without such a clause, a court might allow a reasonable time.

questions.stem: A seller refuses to close on a signed contract. The buyer still wants that specific house. Which remedy best fits?
choices: A suit for the liquidated damages stated in the contract
Rescission of the contract and return of all deposits
Acceptance of the breach without further action
questions.explanation: Each parcel of land is considered unique, so a court may order the seller to perform. Liquidated damages and rescission give the buyer money or an unwinding, not the house.

questions.stem: A buyer defaults, and the purchase contract states the seller's only remedy is to keep the $15,000 earnest money. The seller's actual loss is $25,000. The seller can recover
choices: nothing, because earnest money isn't a remedy
questions.explanation: When the contract makes liquidated damages the sole remedy, the seller is limited to that agreed amount even if actual damages are higher.

questions.stem: A retail tenant pays $2,500 per month base rent plus 5% of annual gross sales over $400,000. Gross sales for the year were $520,000. What is the total annual rent?
A tenant's lease requires her to pay the base rent plus the property taxes, insurance and maintenance. This is a
questions.explanation: In a triple net lease the tenant pays the three main property expenses on top of rent. In a gross lease the landlord pays them.

questions.stem: A tenant's lease ended on June 30. On July 15 he is still in the apartment, has not paid July rent, and the landlord has not agreed to let him stay. He holds a(n)
questions.explanation: A tenant who stays after the lease ends without the landlord's consent holds a tenancy at sufferance, the lowest leasehold estate.

questions.stem: Halfway through a two-year lease, a tenant leaves for a three-month work assignment, planning to return, and rents the apartment to a student for those three months. The student pays rent to the tenant. This arrangement is a(n)
questions.explanation: Transferring only part of the remaining term, with the subtenant paying the original tenant, is a sublease. The original tenant stays liable to the landlord. Transferring the entire remaining term would be an assignment.

questions.stem: Which is a latent defect?
choices: A cracked foundation slab hidden under wall-to-wall carpet
A broken pane in the large front window of the living room
Several missing roof shingles that are visible from the street
A large brown water stain across the middle of the kitchen ceiling
questions.explanation: A latent defect is hidden and wouldn't be found by ordinary inspection. The other choices are visible on a walk-through, making them patent defects.

questions.stem: A home built in 1965 is being sold. Under the federal lead-based paint rule, what must the seller give the buyer before the buyer is bound by the contract?
choices: A clearance certificate from a certified inspector showing the home is lead-free
The EPA pamphlet, known lead information and records, and a chance to inspect
Proof from a licensed abatement contractor that all lead-based paint was removed
A written warranty from the seller that no lead-based paint hazards exist in the home
questions.explanation: The rule requires disclosure, not removal or testing by the seller: the pamphlet, known lead information and reports, the warning statement, and a 10-day inspection opportunity unless waived or changed.

questions.stem: Under the federal lead-based paint rule, how long must the seller and agents keep copies of the signed disclosure?
questions.explanation: Sellers, landlords and agents must keep the signed disclosure records for 3 years after closing or the start of the lease.

questions.stem: At what radon level does the EPA recommend that homeowners fix their home?
questions.explanation: The EPA recommends fixing a home at 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) or higher, and suggests considering mitigation between 2 and 4 pCi/L.

questions.stem: During a showing a broker notices two capped pipes sticking out of the ground in the backyard of a property once heated with fuel oil. What should the broker do?
choices: Say nothing, because the pipes are a patent condition the buyer can see
Assure the buyer that old fuel oil tanks are almost always empty and safe
Have the pipes cut off and removed before the next scheduled showing
Disclose the observation and recommend an inspection for a buried tank
questions.explanation: Fill and vent pipes can indicate an underground storage tank, which can leak. Brokers should disclose what they observe and recommend an expert, never conceal or dismiss it.

questions.stem: Under CERCLA, a company buys an industrial lot and later learns a prior owner buried solvents there. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Only the party that actually caused the contamination can be held liable for it
Liability covers only contamination that occurred after the current owner bought
The current owner can be liable for cleanup even though it didn't cause it
The EPA must prove the current owner was negligent before it can recover costs
questions.explanation: CERCLA liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive, so current owners can be liable for contamination they didn't cause, subject to limited defenses.

questions.stem: Before buying a commercial site, a buyer orders a Phase I environmental site assessment mainly to
choices: support an appeal seeking a lower property tax assessment for the site
support a CERCLA defense by showing all appropriate inquiry
satisfy the Statute of Frauds requirement for a written purchase contract
replace the title commitment and survey normally used at closing
questions.explanation: A Phase I assessment investigates past uses and possible contamination. It supports the innocent landowner defense and similar defenses under CERCLA.

questions.stem: Asbestos insulation in a building is in good condition and not crumbling. What is often the recommended approach?
choices: Leave it in place or encapsulate it, with professional guidance
Have the owner scrape it off immediately so it can't cause harm
Paint over it without any assessment and disclose nothing to buyers
Tell buyers that intact asbestos is never a health concern at all
questions.explanation: Asbestos is most dangerous when friable. Intact material is often safer left in place or encapsulated, and any work should be done by qualified professionals.

questions.stem: A buyer is financing a home with a federally backed mortgage. The home is in a FEMA special flood hazard area (Zone AE). Which is true?
choices: Flood insurance is optional because it's only a 100-year floodplain
The lender will require flood insurance
Flood insurance is required only if the home flooded before
The broker must buy the flood policy for the buyer
questions.explanation: Properties in special flood hazard areas (1% annual chance) financed with federally backed or regulated loans must carry flood insurance.

cards.front: Five essential elements of a real estate contract
cards.back: Competent parties, offer and acceptance, consideration, legal purpose, and a writing (Statute of Frauds).
Requires contracts for the sale of real property (and, in many states, leases over one year) to be in writing and signed to be enforceable.
Promise for a promise; both parties bound. Example: purchase contract.
Promise for an act; only one party bound. Example: option before exercise.
Express: terms stated in words (oral or written). Implied: created by the parties' conduct.
Executory: obligations remain. Executed: fully performed (e.g., after closing).
No legal effect at all. Examples: illegal purpose; party previously adjudicated incompetent.
Valid until the protected party disaffirms. Examples: minor's contract; fraud, duress, undue influence.
Appears valid but a court won't enforce it — e.g., an oral real estate sales contract or one past the statute of limitations.
Voidable by the minor only; the adult stays bound.
Fraud is intentional deception about a material fact; misrepresentation can be innocent or negligent. Both can make a contract voidable.
Duress: threats or force. Undue influence: abusing a position of trust or control.
Mutual mistake of a material fact can void a contract; a one-sided mistake usually doesn't.
Vague opinion or exaggeration ("best view in town"); not misrepresentation because it isn't a statement of fact.
Something of legal value exchanged — money or a promise. Earnest money isn't required; the promise to pay is consideration.
Rejects and ends the original offer and creates a new offer with roles reversed.

cards.front: When can an offer be revoked?
cards.back: Any time before acceptance is communicated to the offeror, even if it says it will stay open (unless it's an option).
Acceptance, rejection, counteroffer, revocation, expiration, death or incapacity of a party, destruction of the property.
When the unconditional acceptance is communicated (delivered) to the offeror or the offeror's agent.
Acceptance must match the offer exactly; any change makes it a counteroffer.
Present all offers promptly; the seller decides. Don't share terms with other buyers without seller permission.
Give electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper when parties agree to transact electronically.
Optionee pays for the right (not obligation) to buy at a set price within a set time; optionor must sell if exercised.
Optionor = owner who grants the option and is bound. Optionee = holder of the right to buy.
Right to match a third-party offer if the owner decides to sell. No set price; owner can't be forced to sell.
Assignment: assignor stays secondarily liable. Novation: new contract/party; original party released.

cards.front: Can a listing agreement be assigned?
cards.back: Generally no without consent — it's a personal service contract with the broker.
Condition that must be satisfied before a party must perform (financing, appraisal, inspection, sale of home).
Makes contract deadlines strict; missing one is a breach.
Addendum: added when the contract is signed. Amendment: changes the contract after formation; all parties sign.
Court order to perform as promised; mainly a buyer's remedy because land is unique.
Damages amount agreed in advance; commonly the earnest money. Must be reasonable, not a penalty.
Money to cover the actual loss caused by a breach.
Cancels the contract and returns parties to their original positions.
Deadline to file suit; after it runs the claim is unenforceable. Length varies by state.
Performance, mutual release, novation, impossibility, operation of law, breach.
The buyer's interest under a signed purchase contract before closing; seller still holds legal title.
Lease with a definite beginning and end; ends automatically, no notice needed.
Renews automatically period to period (e.g., month-to-month) until proper notice.

cards.front: Tenancy at will vs. at sufferance
cards.back: At will: no set term, both consent, ends on notice or death. At sufferance: holdover without landlord consent.
Gross: landlord pays property expenses. Net: tenant pays some or all (triple net = taxes, insurance, maintenance).
Base rent plus a percentage of gross sales, often over a threshold; typical in retail.
Ground: land only, tenant builds. Graduated: scheduled step increases. Index: rent tied to an index such as CPI.
Lease option: tenant may buy. Lease-purchase: tenant agrees to buy.

cards.front: Assignment vs. sublease of a lease
cards.back: Assignment: entire remaining interest; assignee pays landlord. Sublease: part of interest; subtenant pays original tenant.
A fact that would affect a reasonable buyer's decision or the price paid.
Latent: hidden, not found by ordinary inspection — must be disclosed if known. Patent: visible on reasonable inspection.
Property with a psychological stigma (death, crime, illness) but no physical defect. Colorado: not a material fact requiring disclosure (C.R.S. 38-35.5-101).
Most housing built before 1978.
10 days to inspect or do a risk assessment; may be changed by written agreement or waived.
3 years after closing or the start of the lease.
Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home.
EPA: fix the home at 4 pCi/L or higher.
Crumbling asbestos that releases fibers — the dangerous condition. Intact asbestos is often left or encapsulated.
Strict, joint and several, and retroactive; current owners can be liable for past contamination.
Review of past uses and records to identify possible contamination; supports CERCLA defenses.
Protected under the Clean Water Act; filling usually requires an Army Corps of Engineers permit.
FEMA zone (A or V) with 1% annual flood chance; flood insurance required with federally backed or federally regulated loans.

cards.front: Broker response to a suspected hazard
cards.back: Disclose what you observed and recommend an expert inspection.

glossary.definition: The legal ability to enter a contract: being of legal age and mentally competent.
A proposal showing willingness to be bound on definite terms, which becomes a contract when accepted.
The offeree's unconditional agreement to the exact terms of an offer, communicated to the offeror.
Something of legal value — money, property, or a promise — exchanged by each party to a contract.
Law requiring certain contracts, including contracts to sell real estate, to be in writing and signed to be enforceable.
A contract whose terms are stated in words, oral or written.
A contract created by the parties' conduct rather than stated words.
A contract in which each party exchanges a promise and both are obligated.
A contract in which one party promises something in exchange for an act; only that party is bound.
A contract with obligations still to be performed.
A contract that all parties have fully performed.
An agreement with no legal effect, such as one for an illegal purpose.
A contract that is valid until the protected party chooses to cancel it, such as one signed by a minor.
A false statement of material fact that the other party relies on; it may be innocent, negligent or intentional.
Intentional misstatement or concealment of a material fact to induce someone to act, causing them harm.
Forcing a person to agree through threats or force; makes a contract voidable.
Using a position of trust or control to obtain someone's agreement unfairly; makes a contract voidable.
A written document authorizing one person (the attorney-in-fact) to act for another.
A response that changes an offer's terms; it rejects the original offer and becomes a new offer.
Federal law (2000) giving electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper ones.
aliases: Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act

glossary.definition: The Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, a state law adopted by nearly all states that validates electronic records and signatures.
A contract giving the optionee the right, but not the obligation, to buy property at a set price within a set time, for consideration.
The right to match a third-party offer before the owner sells to that third party.
Transfer of a party's contract rights (and usually duties) to another; the assignor stays secondarily liable.
Replacing a contract or party with a new one by agreement, releasing the original party.
A condition that must be met before a party is obligated to perform under a contract.
Contract clause making deadlines strict, so missing one is a breach.
Additional material attached to and made part of a contract when it is signed.
A change to the terms of an existing contract, signed by all parties after the contract is formed.
Failure to perform a contract promise without legal excuse.
A court order requiring a party to perform as promised; used because land is unique.
An amount of damages agreed in advance in the contract, often the earnest money.
Canceling a contract and returning the parties to their original positions.
A buyer's good-faith deposit with an offer, held in trust and often used as liquidated damages if the buyer defaults.
The deadline set by state law for filing a lawsuit; after it passes, the claim can't be enforced.
A buyer's interest in property under a signed purchase contract before legal title passes at closing.
A tenant's non-freehold right to possess property for a period under a lease.
A leasehold with a definite start and end date that ends automatically without notice.
A leasehold that renews automatically for successive periods, such as month to month, until notice is given.
A leasehold of no fixed term that lasts as long as both parties wish.
Occupancy by a tenant who stays after the lease ends without the landlord's consent.
A lease where the tenant pays fixed rent and the landlord pays property expenses.
A lease where the tenant pays rent plus some or all of the property's expenses.
A net lease where the tenant pays rent plus property taxes, insurance and maintenance.
A lease with base rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales, common in retail.
A long-term lease of land only, on which the tenant usually builds.
A lease with rent that increases in scheduled steps.
A lease whose rent adjusts with an economic index, such as the Consumer Price Index.
A lease that gives the tenant the right, but not the obligation, to buy the property.
A tenant's transfer of part of its leasehold interest; the original tenant remains liable and acts as the subtenant's landlord.
"Let the buyer beware" — the old rule that buyers must discover defects themselves.
A fact that would affect a reasonable person's decision to buy or the price they'd pay.
A hidden defect not discoverable by ordinary inspection.
Property that buyers may avoid for psychological reasons, such as a death or crime there, rather than physical defects.
Federal rule requiring sellers and landlords of most pre-1978 housing to disclose known lead-based paint hazards and give the EPA pamphlet.
A naturally occurring, odorless radioactive gas from uranium decay in soil; EPA action level is 4 pCi/L.
A fibrous mineral once used in building materials that is hazardous when friable (crumbling).
A buried tank holding fuel or chemicals that can leak and contaminate soil and groundwater.
Insulation used in the 1970s that can release formaldehyde gas.
Land saturated with water much of the time, protected under the Clean Water Act.
The Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (Superfund), imposing strict, joint and several, retroactive cleanup liability.
aliases: Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act

glossary.definition: A study of a property's history and records to identify possible contamination, used to support CERCLA defenses.
FEMA-mapped area with a 1% annual chance of flooding (Zones A and V); flood insurance required with federally backed or federally regulated loans.
